name: cover-title
text: Can a message point to its own mistake?
textPreview: Can a message point to its own mistake?

name: text
text: Today you will design the idea—not just learn the recipe.
textPreview: Today you will design the idea—not just learn the recipe.

alt: Seven binary tiles travel through three scanning beams; one tile is visibly corrupted

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Ask students to inspect the image. What could the three beams be doing? Do not name parity or Hamming codes. Say: our goal is to invent a message that helps the receiver locate one damaged bit.


[Sources]
- Hero illustration generated for this deck with OpenAI ImageGen on 2026-08-25; no external asset.
- Session theme continues the local GLITCH! math-circle deck in this workspace.
[/Sources]

name: title-2
text: Why can’t the receiver recover a missing bit?
textPreview: Why can’t the receiver recover a missing bit?

name: text
text: Both 0 and 1 fit what the receiver can see.
textPreview: Both 0 and 1 fit what the receiver can see.

name: text
text: Once information disappears, clever guessing cannot bring it back.
textPreview: Once information disappears, clever guessing cannot bring it back.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Give silent think time, then pairs. Ask for two different original messages consistent with the damaged string. The proof of impossibility is that both choices fit. The design lesson: correction requires redundancy sent before the damage happens. Worksheet 1A.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-3
text: What must the extra bits tell us?
textPreview: What must the extra bits tell us?

name: text
text: The channel may flip at most one of seven transmitted bits.
textPreview: The channel may flip at most one of seven transmitted bits.

name: text
text: The receiver must distinguish eight possible states.
textPreview: The receiver must distinguish eight possible states.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Have students count the possibilities aloud: one no-error state plus seven possible error positions. Ask what kind of information could name one of eight states. Do not answer yet.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-4
text: Why isn’t one parity check enough?
textPreview: Why isn’t one parity check enough?

name: text
text: After one flip, parity changes to odd.
textPreview: After one flip, parity changes to odd.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Model even parity, then use Worksheet 1B. Ask students to imagine each of four positions flipping: every case makes parity odd. One parity answer collapses all error locations into the same alarm. Detection is not location.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-5
text: Why are three yes/no checks exactly enough?
textPreview: Why are three yes/no checks exactly enough?

name: text
text: Three answers can name exactly: no error + seven positions.
textPreview: Three answers can name exactly: no error + seven positions.

name: text
text: Could you invent eight different three-answer fingerprints?
textPreview: Could you invent eight different three-answer fingerprints?

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Let students predict the third number before revealing 8. Each yes/no question doubles the number of distinguishable cases. Three is both sufficient and minimal for eight states. This is the first reason Hamming(7,4) needs three check bits.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-6
text: Can you invent seven unique error fingerprints?
textPreview: Can you invent seven unique error fingerprints?

name: text
text: Give each state a different pattern of three answers.
textPreview: Give each state a different pattern of three answers.

name: text
text: Rule: no two columns may match.
textPreview: Rule: no two columns may match.

text:
Timing: 6 minutes.

Pairs invent eight distinct three-answer patterns on scrap paper or Worksheet 1C. Do not insist on binary order. After three minutes, compare designs: all successful solutions use every possible pattern exactly once. Ask which pattern naturally means no error.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-7
text: Binary gives every state a three-answer name
textPreview: Binary gives every state a three-answer name

name: text
text: Each position’s number is also its answer fingerprint.
textPreview: Each position’s number is also its answer fingerprint.

name: text
text: Read the three answers as the 4s, 2s, and 1s digits.
textPreview: Read the three answers as the 4s, 2s, and 1s digits.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Reveal binary as a naming convenience, not a prerequisite. Read 6 as 110: yes to the 4-question, yes to the 2-question, no to the 1-question. Students may instead think of adding labels 4+2.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-8
text: The names tell us what each question must cover
textPreview: The names tell us what each question must cover

name: text
text: Question 1 asks about positions whose 1s digit is 1; question 2 uses the 2s digit; question 4 uses the 4s digit.
textPreview: Question 1 asks about positions whose 1s digit is 1; question 2 uses the 2s digit; question 4 uses the 4s digit.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Before showing each row, ask students to derive it from the binary names. Position 5=101 belongs to questions 1 and 4. Position 7=111 belongs to all three. The overlapping sets are not magic; they are the columns of the address system.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-9
text: Three questions can locate someone you cannot see
textPreview: Three questions can locate someone you cannot see

text:
Timing: 6 minutes.

Play with seven volunteers or pairs choosing secret positions. Ask only the three fixed membership questions. Students should experience the address pattern identifying the position before parity is introduced as the way to store those answers in a transmitted message.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-10
text: Why parity makes the questions travel with the message
textPreview: Why parity makes the questions travel with the message

name: text
text: Choose its check bit so the group is EVEN.
textPreview: Choose its check bit so the group is EVEN.

name: text
text: That question’s answer changes from no to yes.
textPreview: That question’s answer changes from no to yes.

name: text
text: Parity works because every single flip toggles odd/even.
textPreview: Parity works because every single flip toggles odd/even.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Ask why even/odd is a good stored answer. A single bit flip changes a count by exactly one, so it always toggles parity. Each check group carries one durable yes/no answer. The three answers together carry an address.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-11
text: A self-checking message needs three adjustable bits
textPreview: A self-checking message needs three adjustable bits

name: text
text: Four slots hold the message. Three slots are knobs that force the three parity promises to be true.
textPreview: Four slots hold the message. Three slots are knobs that force the three parity promises to be true.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Ask students to identify how many adjustable bits are needed to set three independent parity answers. The data bits are fixed by the message; the check bits are the three available knobs.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-12
text: Why the check bits live at positions 1, 2, and 4
textPreview: Why the check bits live at positions 1, 2, and 4

name: text
text: Each check bit changes only its own parity equation.
textPreview: Each check bit changes only its own parity equation.

name: text
text: That is why powers of two are the cleanest places for the knobs.
textPreview: That is why powers of two are the cleanest places for the knobs.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

This is the crucial why behind positions 1,2,4. Their binary addresses contain exactly one 1, so each belongs to only one check group. Adjusting p1 cannot disturb checks 2 or 4, and similarly for the others.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-13
text: Can we practice with one data slot locked?
textPreview: Can we practice with one data slot locked?

name: text
text: Use three message bits in positions 3, 5, 6. Fix position 7 at zero.
textPreview: Use three message bits in positions 3, 5, 6. Fix position 7 at zero.

name: text
text: This is practice inside the full machine—not a standard Hamming(7,3) code.
textPreview: This is practice inside the full machine—not a standard Hamming(7,3) code.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Explain that locking one data slot reduces cognitive load without changing the check groups. Worksheet 2B uses this restricted subcode.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: For each question: count the known 1s, then choose its knob to make the total even.
textPreview: For each question: count the known 1s, then choose its knob to make the total even.

name: prompt-badge-text
text: WHY CAN EACH KNOB BE SOLVED SEPARATELY?
textPreview: WHY CAN EACH KNOB BE SOLVED SEPARATELY?

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Pairs solve 101. Use a hint ladder rather than giving formulas. Ask the displayed why: positions 1,2,4 each belong only to their own question. Expected p1=1, p2=0, p4=1. Worksheet 2B.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-15
text: Every check is even because we chose it that way
textPreview: Every check is even because we chose it that way

name: text
text: The codeword carries three promises about itself.
textPreview: The codeword carries three promises about itself.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Have three students each audit one group. Ask what the receiver expects before any error: three even totals, equivalent to fingerprint 000.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-16
text: Why seven protected bits carry at most four data bits
textPreview: Why seven protected bits carry at most four data bits

name: text
text: one clean word + seven one-flip versions
textPreview: one clean word + seven one-flip versions

name: text
text: Hamming(7,4) fills the space exactly: no room is wasted.
textPreview: Hamming(7,4) fills the space exactly: no room is wasted.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Ask each count before revealing it. Every valid codeword must own eight possible received strings: itself and its seven single-bit neighbors. The 128 total strings can therefore protect at most 16 messages, exactly four bits. This is the intuitive Hamming bound and why (7,4) is called perfect.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-17
text: Unlocking the final slot gives Hamming(7,4)
textPreview: Unlocking the final slot gives Hamming(7,4)

name: text
text: 3 address bits + 4 message bits = 7 transmitted bits
textPreview: 3 address bits + 4 message bits = 7 transmitted bits

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Now the notation should feel earned: seven transmitted positions, four free message bits, and three check bits forced by the parity promises.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-18
text: Can you reconstruct the encoder from its job?
textPreview: Can you reconstruct the encoder from its job?

name: step-body-0
text: Write positions 1–7 and mark 1,2,4 as checks.
textPreview: Write positions 1–7 and mark 1,2,4 as checks.

name: step-body-1
text: Put the four message bits in 3,5,6,7.
textPreview: Put the four message bits in 3,5,6,7.

name: step-body-2
text: Choose p₁,p₂,p₄ so their groups are even.
textPreview: Choose p₁,p₂,p₄ so their groups are even.

name: step-body-3
text: Verify all three expected answers are NO.
textPreview: Verify all three expected answers are NO.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Ask students to propose the steps before revealing them. The routine should be reconstructed from the purpose of the code, not memorized as an arbitrary recipe. Worksheet 3A.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: Builder chooses the three knobs. Auditor explains why each promise is true.
textPreview: Builder chooses the three knobs. Auditor explains why each promise is true.

name: prompt-badge-text
text: WORKSHEET 3B • DO NOT GUESS THE CHECK BITS
textPreview: WORKSHEET 3B • DO NOT GUESS THE CHECK BITS

text:
Timing: 6 minutes.

Pairs encode 1011. Require reasoning in terms of the three questions. Expected p1=0, p2=1, p4=0. The auditor must explain why each even total means the receiver will expect a no-error fingerprint of 000.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-20
text: Three checks prove the codeword is ready
textPreview: Three checks prove the codeword is ready

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Verify each group. Ask where the original data is hiding: positions 3,5,6,7. The all-pass fingerprint 000 is now visibly built into the word.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: If two teammates disagree, audit the three promises instead of voting.
textPreview: If two teammates disagree, audit the three promises instead of voting.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Teams divide Worksheet 3C and cross-audit. Answers: 0000000; 1111111; 0100101; 0111100. The point is transfer: the groups and logic remain fixed while the message changes.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: When you return: we use the same three questions to find a flip.
textPreview: When you return: we use the same three questions to find a flip.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Take a real five-minute break. Resume by asking: Why were three questions enough? Why were positions 1,2,4 special?

name: text
text: Do not hunt by eye. Ask the same three parity questions.
textPreview: Do not hunt by eye. Ask the same three parity questions.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Students run the checks on Worksheet 4A. Q1 passes with two ones; Q2 and Q4 fail with three ones. Ask why a flipped bit changes exactly the questions that contain its position.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-24
text: Why the failed questions spell the error address
textPreview: Why the failed questions spell the error address

name: text
text: The error reproduces the fingerprint of its position.
textPreview: The error reproduces the fingerprint of its position.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

This is the core explanation of the syndrome. Position 6 belongs to Q2 and Q4, so a flip there makes exactly those questions fail. The failed-answer pattern is 110, the binary name of 6. Adding failed labels is simply another way to read the same address.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-25
text: Why one flip repairs the word
textPreview: Why one flip repairs the word

name: text
text: The second flip toggles the same checks back to even.
textPreview: The second flip toggles the same checks back to even.

name: text
text: Repair first. Then read the message from positions 3, 5, 6, 7.
textPreview: Repair first. Then read the message from positions 3, 5, 6, 7.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Ask students to explain why flipping the addressed bit, rather than replacing it with a guessed value, works. A binary flip is its own inverse. Then emphasize repair before extraction.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: Explain why the failed-question fingerprint identifies the bit.
textPreview: Explain why the failed-question fingerprint identifies the bit.

text:
Timing: 6 minutes.

Packet A: only Q4 fails → position 4 → corrected 0100101 → message 0101. Packet B: all fail → position 7 → corrected 0111100 → message 1100. Require the causal explanation, not only the arithmetic.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-27
text: Invent a codeword your partner can rescue
textPreview: Invent a codeword your partner can rescue

name: step-body-3
text: Partner repairs it and justifies the address.
textPreview: Partner repairs it and justifies the address.

name: text
text: A successful rescue reproduces the sender’s message for the right reason.
textPreview: A successful rescue reproduces the sender’s message for the right reason.

text:
Timing: 6 minutes.

Use Worksheet 5. Keep this shorter than the previous deck so there is time for the conceptual why. Receivers must say which parity questions failed and why those answers name the sender’s secret position.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-28
text: Why two errors can impersonate a third
textPreview: Why two errors can impersonate a third

name: text
text: An eighth overall parity bit separates odd flips from even flips.
textPreview: An eighth overall parity bit separates odd flips from even flips.

name: text
text: That is the intuition behind extended Hamming(8,4).
textPreview: That is the intuition behind extended Hamming(8,4).

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Show why the one-error promise matters: two error fingerprints XOR into another valid address. The optional eighth overall parity bit reveals whether the total number of flips is odd or even, enabling double-error detection.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-29
text: Can you do the whole job alone?
textPreview: Can you do the whole job alone?

name: text
text: Explain why all three checks pass.
textPreview: Explain why all three checks pass.

name: text
text: Explain why the syndrome names the error.
textPreview: Explain why the syndrome names the error.

name: text
text: Method matters: roles → parity promises → address → repair → extract
textPreview: Method matters: roles → parity promises → address → repair → extract

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Students work independently. Part A: 0011001. Part B: Q1 and Q4 fail → position 5 → corrected 0011001 → message 1001. Score the explanation as well as the result.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: You did not memorize Hamming(7,4). You derived it.
textPreview: You did not memorize Hamming(7,4). You derived it.

name: text
text: Check: Part A 0011001 • Part B error at 5 → message 1001
textPreview: Check: Part A 0011001 • Part B error at 5 → message 1001

name: text
text: Exit whisper: Which design choice now feels inevitable?
textPreview: Exit whisper: Which design choice now feels inevitable?

text:
Timing: 1 minute.

Students name one why they can now explain: three checks, the overlap sets, positions 1/2/4, or the syndrome. The close resolves the opening question: the message points to damage because its three parity promises form an address.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]
